'''''Arthrocaulon macrostachyum''''', [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] '''''Arthrocnemum macrostachyum''''', is a [[species]] of flowering plant in the [[Amaranthaceae|amaranth family]]. It is native to coastal areas of the [[Mediterranean Sea]] and the [[Red Sea]] and parts of the [[Middle East]], where it grows in coastal and inland [[salt marsh]]es, [[Dry lake|alkali flats]], and other habitats with [[Soil salinity|saline soils]].

==Description==
''Arthrocaulon macrostachyum'' is a much-branched [[shrub|subshrub]] growing in clumps up to a metre high (3 ft). The plants have horizontal woody stems that may root at the nodes, branching into erect, jointed, succulent green stems. The [[Leaf|leaves]] are small and scale-like, clasping the stem but with the tips free. The flowers are minute, produced in threes in terminal, cylindrical spikes. The [[perianth]] is conical and has three teeth. The [[hermaphrodite]] [[flower]]s are wind-pollinated, and the [[fruit]] is small, has a membranous [[Fruit anatomy|pericarp]], and contains a single seed.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://plants.jstor.org/compilation/arthrocnemum.macrostachyum |title= ''Arthrocnemum macrostachyum'' |website= Global Plants |publisher= JSTOR |accessdate=5 February 2016}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''A. macrostachyum'' is found around the coasts bordering on the Mediterranean Sea and the Red Sea, and ranges northwards into the [[Jordan Rift Valley|Jordan Valley]]. It is also present in the Middle East, including Iran and Pakistan, where it grows in the muddy coastal swamps immediately inland from the [[mangroves]] (''[[Avicennia marina]]'') that border the coast.<ref name=Ahmad>{{cite book |author1=Ahmad, R. |author2=Malik, K.A. |title= Prospects for Saline Agriculture |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=6s3rCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA353 |year=2013 |publisher= Springer Science & Business Media |isbn= 978-94-017-0067-2 |pages= 353–363}}</ref> In the delta region of the Mediterranean coast of Egypt, it dominates some plant communities in the [[salt marsh]] habitats.<ref>{{cite journal |author1= Zahran, M.A. |author2= El-Demerdash, M.A. |author3= Mashaly, I.A. |year=1990 |title= Vegetation types of the deltaic Mediterranean coast of Egypt and their environment |journal=Journal of Vegetation Science |volume=1 |issue=3 |pages=305–310 |doi=10.2307/3235705 |jstor= 3235705 }}</ref>

==Research==
In a study, plants of ''A. macrostachyum'' were germinated at six [[sodium chloride]] (NaCl) concentrations, and grew best at 200 to 400 mM NaCl.<ref name=Khan/> It was found that the plants were salt-tolerant and grew well at a range of salt concentrations. About 60% of their dry mass was ash, and the plants were capable of accumulating a substantial quantity of sodium and chlorine ions.<ref name="Khan">{{cite journal |author1= Khan, M. Ajmal |author2=Ungar, Irwin A. |author3= Showalter, Allan M. |year=2005 |title= Salt Stimulation and Tolerance in an Intertidal Stem-Succulent Halophyte |journal=Journal of Plant Nutrition |volume= 28 |issue=8 |pages= 1365–1374 |doi= 10.1081/PLN-200067462 |s2cid=42028819 }}</ref> The seeds of many [[halophyte]]s germinate after rains which reduce the salinity levels of the soil surface layer. ''A. macrostachyum'' can germinate at salinity levels of at least 800 mM NaCl, and at even higher concentrations in the presence of added calcium ions.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Khan, M. Ajmal |author2= Weber. Darrell J. |title= Ecophysiology of High Salinity Tolerant Plants |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=5SlrbUaec0gC&pg=PA108 |year=2006 |publisher= Springer Science & Business Media |isbn= 978-1-4020-4018-4 |page=108}}</ref>

Research was undertaken into the remediation of oil-contaminated soil in the Persian Gulf. The marshland concerned was covered by an algal mat but was otherwise vegetation-free. The creation of drainage channels was followed by the return of [[crab]]s to the affected areas close to the channels. They churned up the mud and increased the oxygen content, which was quickly followed by the germination of ''A. macrostachyum'', ''[[Halocnemum strobilaceum]]'' and ''[[Salicornia europaea]]''. The crabs advanced into the polluted area at the rate of about one metre per year (3 ft), resulting in a gradual increase in the vegetated area.<ref name=Abuzinada>{{cite book |author1=Abdulaziz H. Abuzinada |author2= Hans-Jörg Barth |author3=Friedhelm Krupp |author4= Benno Böer Thabit |author5= Zahran Al Abdessalaam |title= Protecting the Gulf's Marine Ecosystems from Pollution |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=8vMzKsGikTkC&pg=PA270 |year=2008 |publisher= Springer Science & Business Media |isbn= 978-3-7643-7947-6 |page= 270}}</ref>

''A. macrostachyum'' tolerates levels of [[cadmium]] in the soil that other plants find toxic. It can [[Bioaccumulation|bioaccumulate]] the metal and play a role in the [[phytoremediation]] of sites contaminated by cadmium.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Redondo-Gómez, Susana |author2= Mateos-Naranjo, Enrique |author3=Andrades-Moreno, Luis |year=2010 |title= Accumulation and tolerance characteristics of cadmium in a halophytic Cd-hyperaccumulator, ''Arthrocnemum macrostachyum'' |journal= Journal of Hazardous Materials |volume=184 |issue=1–3 |pages= 299–307 |doi= 10.1016/j.jhazmat.2010.08.036 |pmid= 20832167 }}</ref>

The seeds of ''A. macrostachyum'' contain between 22% and 25% oil, with an unsaturated [[fatty acid]] content of 65% to 74%, and are being investigated as a possible source of edible oil.<ref>{{cite journal |author1= Weber, D.J. |author2=Ansari, R. |author3= Gul, B. |author4= Khan, M. Ajmal |year=2007 |title= Potential of halophytes as source of edible oil |journal= Journal of Arid Environments |volume=68 |issue=2 |pages=315–321 |doi= 10.1016/j.jaridenv.2006.05.010 |bibcode=2007JArEn..68..315W }}</ref>
